newsitem.title: SPAIN: Celebrity trial of disgraced Spanish banker begins.
newsitem.headline: Celebrity trial of disgraced Spanish banker begins.

text.p: Spain's fallen banking hero Mario Conde, accused of fraud in the 1993 collapse of the Banesto bank he chaired, walked into a Madrid court on Monday for the start of one of the country's most keenly anticipated trials.
Meticulously groomed in a dark suit and his trademark slicked-back hair, Conde looked straight ahead and did not respond to questions from the many journalists and spectators at the entrance.
The once-eminent banker and his closest collaborators are accused of fraud, falsification and misappropriation in what has become Spain's biggest case of financial crime.

The High Court's investigating judge said they hid the true financial state of Banco Espanol de Credito-Banesto, which ran up a deficit of 605 billion pesetas ($4.25 billion) in 1993, and were directly to blame for the bank's crisis.
The hearing on Monday is only a small piece in the multi-trial Banesto jigsaw and marks the beginning of what Spanish media are saying will be a long, drawn-out process.
It concerns a 600 million peseta payment made in 1990 by Banesto to Argentia Trust, a mysterious company based on the tax haven island of Saint Vincent in the Antilles.
Conde is charged with misappropriation of the funds and falsification of documents connected to the payment and faces seven years in jail if convicted.
He says the payment went to a well-connected intermediary, Antonio Navalon, who helped Banesto get approval from Spain's former Socialist government for some business deals.
He denies he ever asked Navalon to make payments to anyone in the government or the government party.
The case has been riddled with peculiarities.
The judge who formally charged Conde first ordered his detention and then reversed the decision three hours later and ordered Conde's release. The judge was subsequently sacked.
Conde's lawyers have said they will argue that the charge was unfounded, the High Court was not competent to try the case and the rights of the accused have been abused.
The trial, which commentators view as minor compared to the others facing the ex-financier, is expected to last nine days.

The central Banesto case, in which Conde is accused of syphoning off 300 million pesetas from Banesto accounts for his personal use, is not expected to start before October. He faces 35 to 44 years prison if convicted in that trial.
Conde, a lawyer who sprang from nowhere to buy his way on to the Banesto board in 1987, was at the helm of the bank for six years before he and his board were effectively sacked by the Bank of Spain.

A parliament committee investigating the bank's collapse, which cost the state 192 billion pesetas to bail out, said it was due in part to Conde's aggressive campaign to build up Banesto's loan portfolio just as a recession started to bite.
But the committee also felt the level of bad debts had been concealed from shareholders and auditors.
